issues.title: obfsgen: a generative approach towards tunnel obfuscation
issues.body:
Hey folks, we'd like to share a research prototype here and (hopefully) get the community's opinions on it.
(Yes, we're aware of #674, and we have to admit that we used AI for coding. We try to respect other people's time, so we tried to describe the design in the README as clearly as we could, so that anyone curious can get the gist of the idea without reading the code.)

**TL;DR:** obfsgen is our attempt to answer "what a tunnel should look like shape-wise" (i.e., record sizes and timing), using generative models.

[Repo](https://github.com/goose-lab-cuhk/obfsgen) · [Preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15019)

**Q: What is obfsgen?**

A: obfsgen is an obfuscation tool for tunneled traffic. Unlike existing obfuscators, obfsgen takes a generative approach to obfuscation, in which it trains a model on traffic that is considered *normal* and then shapes the tunneled traffic towards that normality.

**Q: Why yet another obfuscator?**

A: The design principle of obfsgen is to decouple the obfuscation layer from the application layer. Existing obfuscators are *application-driven*, in that each `write()` of the application triggers the obfuscation layer to pad, split or delay the data it is handed. Such an obfuscator can only add to the shape the application creates, so bursts can grow and delays can lengthen but never the reverse (below some links explained this much better than us). obfsgen instead keeps its own schedule of 1) when to send each TLS record and 2) how large the record is, independent of the application. The application's bytes fill the scheduled records, which are padded when there is nothing to send, so the tunnel can send before the application writes, keep sending while the application is idle, and hold data back while the schedule demands quiet time.

![Application-driven and application-independent obfuscators](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/goose-lab-cuhk/obfsgen/main/docs/figures/app-driven-vs-independent.png)

Practitioners have argued for an obfuscator like this for years:
- In 2017, David Fifield showed that obfs4 could queue Tor's data in a send buffer and send it on a schedule of its own, with padding when the buffer is empty, and released a proof of concept that sends at a constant rate ([tor-dev](https://lists.torproject.org/pipermail/tor-dev/2017-June/012310.html)).
- In 2019, Fifield wrote that "a separate timing/size protocol is needed", which sends a data packet when the packet-size scheduler leaves room for it and padding otherwise ([net4people/bbs#9](https://github.com/net4people/bbs/issues/9#issuecomment-524095186)).
- In 2023, the developer of Restls argued that padding "can only increase the length of the packets" and leaves the pattern of the TLS handshake unchanged, and proposed scripts that set the length of each early packet, padding shorter data and truncating longer data ([Restls-Script](https://github.com/3andne/restls/blob/main/Restls-Script%3A%20Hide%20Your%20Proxy%20Traffic%20Behavior.md)).
- In 2024, researchers evaluated how well encapsulated TLS handshakes (TLS over TLS) identify obfuscated proxy traffic, and discussed why obfuscation that depends on the application cannot remove them, since padding and multiplexing reduce neither the size of bursts nor the number of round trips ([USENIX Security 2024](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity24/presentation/xue-fingerprinting)). In 2025, it was shown that because the timing obfuscation of obfs4 is application-driven, it makes the timing fingerprint of proxy traffic more pronounced, not less ([NDSS 2025](https://www.ndss-symposium.org/ndss-paper/the-discriminative-power-of-cross-layer-rtts-in-fingerprinting-proxy-traffic/)).

issues.title: SAM: subsessions of a MASTER session send all datagrams with the first subsession's version (breaks BitTorrent UDP tracker announces)
issues.body:
**Version:** 3.0.0 (docker `purplei2p/i2pd:release-3.0.0`). The relevant code is unchanged in `openssl` HEAD.

### Context

I'm writing a SAM client that checks **BitTorrent UDP trackers on I2P** (`udp://tracker.i2p:6969/announce` style URLs, supported by I2PSnark since 2.10.0 and by the new i2pd torrents tunnel). The protocol is [BEP 15](https://www.bittorrent.org/beps/bep_0015.html) adapted to I2P by [Prop. 160](https://geti2p.net/spec/proposals/160-udp-trackers) / [udp-announces spec](https://geti2p.net/spec/udp-announces):

| Step | Message | Must be sent as |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Connect request (client -> tracker) | Datagram2 (protocol 19) |
| 2 | Connect response (tracker -> client) | Raw (protocol 18) |
| 3 | Announce request (client -> tracker), using the `connection_id` from step 2 | Datagram3 (protocol 20) |
| 4 | Announce response (tracker -> client) | Raw (protocol 18) |

Steps 1 and 3 must come from **the same destination**, because the tracker binds the `connection_id` to the sender hash. So the client needs a MASTER session with a DATAGRAM2 subsession, a DATAGRAM3 subsession and a RAW subsession.

### Steps to reproduce

```
HELLO VERSION MIN=3.0 MAX=3.3
SESSION CREATE STYLE=MASTER ID=m DESTINATION=TRANSIENT SIGNATURE_TYPE=7
SESSION ADD STYLE=DATAGRAM2 ID=d2 FROM_PORT=6881 LISTEN_PORT=6882 PORT=<udp port> HOST=<udp host>
SESSION ADD STYLE=DATAGRAM3 ID=d3 FROM_PORT=6881 LISTEN_PORT=6883 PORT=<udp port> HOST=<udp host>
SESSION ADD STYLE=RAW ID=r LISTEN_PORT=6881 PORT=<udp port> HOST=<udp host>
```

All subsessions are created OK. Then, via UDP to the SAM UDP port (7655), against the zzzot tracker `opentracker.dg2.i2p` (port 6969):

1. **Connect request** through `d2` (16 bytes: `protocol_id=0x41727101980`, `action=0`, `transaction_id`):
   ```
   3.0 d2 opentracker.dg2.i2p FROM_PORT=6881 TO_PORT=6969\n<connect request>
   ```
   ✅ The tracker replies with a valid connect response (`action=0`, same `transaction_id`, `connection_id`), received on the RAW subsession.

2. **Announce request** through `d3` (98 bytes, `connection_id` from step 1, `action=1`, `info_hash`, `peer_id`, `port=6881`, ...):
   ```
   3.0 d3 opentracker.dg2.i2p FROM_PORT=6881 TO_PORT=6969\n<announce request>
   ```
   ❌ The tracker replies with an error response (`action=3`) and the message `Bad protocol`, i.e. the announce did not arrive as Datagram3.

Other trackers (`opentracker.skank.i2p`, `tracker.insulaocculta.i2p`) behave the same: they answer the connect request but silently drop the announce request.

### Expected

Datagrams sent through the `d3` subsession are sent as Datagram3 (protocol 20), and through `d2` as Datagram2 (protocol 19). According to the SAMv3 spec each subsession of a PRIMARY/MASTER session has its own style.

### Actual

All datagram subsessions send with the version of the **first** datagram subsession added. In the example above `d3` sends Datagram2. If the DATAGRAM3 subsession is added first, then `d2` sends Datagram3 (and the trackers drop the connect request instead).

### Cause

- `ClientDestination::CreateDatagramDestination()` only creates `m_DatagramDestination` once, so the `version` passed by the first subsession wins (`Destination.cpp`).
- `SAMSession::SendDatagram()` -> `DatagramDestination::SendDatagramTo()` -> `ObtainSession()` uses that default version and never applies the sending subsession's `DatagramVersion`.
- Creating two separate sessions with the same keys is not possible either (`DUPLICATED_DEST`).

The built-in torrents tunnel avoids this by calling `session->SetVersion()` per message (`TorrentsTunnel.cpp`: Datagram2 for connect, Datagram3 for announce). SAM could do the same using the sending subsession's `DatagramVersion`.

issues.body:
Each datagram subsession of a MASTER session now sends with its own version, instead of all of them using the version of the first datagram subsession added.

The datagram destination is shared and its default version is fixed by the first subsession, since CreateDatagramDestination is called once. On send, the subsession's stored version is now applied per message through SetVersion, the same way TorrentsTunnel switches between Datagram2 and Datagram3.

Fix for #2638

panic: slice bounds out of range [8192:8171] in XtlsPadding (VLESS outbound, Reality + Vision), recurring ~6x/hour on 25.6.8 / 25.9.5 / 25.12.8
issues.body:
## Summary

A relay node (Xray terminates several inbounds and forwards everything through ONE VLESS+Reality+`xtls-rprx-vision` outbound to another Xray) crashes the whole process several times per hour with a negative-length `Extend` in `proxy.XtlsPadding`. All inbounds are dropped on every crash (about 1 s with `RestartSec=1`).

No `testseed` anywhere in the config (so this is not #5961's "invalid testseed" case). No mux: 0 `v1.mux.cool` connections in the log over 24 h.

## Panic (identical every time, only goroutine ids differ)

```
panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [8192:8171]

goroutine 640 [running]:
github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf.(*Buffer).Extend(...)
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf/buffer.go:153
github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy.XtlsPadding(0xc00021f740, 0x0, 0xc0002e1a28, 0x1?, {0x19a0058, 0xc000254730}, {0xc000269200?, 0xc000730000?, 0xc00033fb40?})
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/proxy.go:519 +0x79e
github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy.(*VisionWriter).WriteMultiBuffer(0xc0002e19e0, {0xc00047ea98, 0x1, 0x1})
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/proxy.go:390 +0x5dd
github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf.copyInternal(...)
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf/copy.go:99 +0x15a
github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf.Copy(...)
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf/copy.go:116
github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/vless/outbound.(*Handler).Process.func4()
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/vless/outbound/outbound.go:360 +0xc79
```

(v25.12.8, go1.25.5, linux/amd64, kernel 6.8, 1 vCPU. `Process.func3` on 25.6.8 — same frames.)

## Analysis

The high bound `8171` is exactly `buf.Size - 21`. In `XtlsPadding`:

```go
if paddingLen > buf.Size-21-contentLen {
    paddingLen = buf.Size - 21 - contentLen
}
...
newbuffer.Extend(paddingLen)
```

`[8192:8171]` means `newbuffer.end == 8192` and `paddingLen == -21`, i.e. `contentLen == 8192`: a full 8192-byte block reached `XtlsPadding` unsplit. `Extend` has no check for negative `n`, so `b.v[b.end:end]` panics with low > high (the `end > len` check only guards the upper side).

`ReshapeMultiBuffer` is supposed to prevent this (it splits every block with `Len() >= buf.Size-21`), and `VisionWriter.WriteMultiBuffer` calls it right before the loop, so a full block should not get through. I could not find the path by reading the code (`XtlsPadding` and `ReshapeMultiBuffer` are byte-identical in v25.12.8 and v26.11.9). Possibilities I could not exclude: a buffer that is mutated/re-used between `ReshapeMultiBuffer` and `XtlsPadding` (pool double-release?), or a block larger than `buf.Size` entering through a non-standard reader.

Cheap hardening regardless of root cause: clamp `paddingLen` at 0 (`if paddingLen < 0 { paddingLen = 0 }`) and/or reject `n < 0` in `Buffer.Extend`. That would turn a process-wide crash into a (harmless) missing padding. Note that `newbuffer.Write(b.Bytes())` also silently truncates if `contentLen + 21 > 8192`, so the root cause is worth fixing too.

## Environment / what was tried

- Topology: several inbounds (Reality-TCP-Vision, Reality-TCP-Vision with self-steal dest, XHTTP+TLS, gRPC+TLS) → one VLESS+Reality+Vision outbound → Xray 25.6.8 server.
- Panics occur with users of ALL four inbounds (so not specific to one inbound transport).
- Versions tried as the relay: 25.6.8 (~1 panic / 5–10 min), 25.9.5 (2 in 1h20m), 25.12.8 (~6 / hour, 434 in 3 days, clustered: up to 5 within a minute). Not yet tried: 26.x on this node (26.10.31/26.11.9 server side breaks sing-box Reality clients in our tests, so we cannot deploy it for production users).
- Config has no `testseed`; `flow: xtls-rprx-vision` only.
- Related: #2651 (same signature, fixed in 2023), #5961 (same signature on 26.2.6/26.3.27, closed with "don't set testseed"), #6072.

## Expected

No process-wide panic on any input to the Vision writer.

issues.title: XDRIVE: when the client disappears mid-download, the server uploads the rest of the response and keeps the session for minutes
issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [X] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [X] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [X] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [X] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [X] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

> 简述：在 v26.10.17（与 main 相同）中，如果 XDRIVE 客户端在下载中途消失（进程被杀或断网），服务端无法察觉：它会继续从目标读取，并把剩余的整个响应写入存储（复现中 20 秒内写入约 235 MiB、607 个对象）。这些对象要等服务端的 mux 子连接自行结束后才会被清理（约 2.7–13 分钟），期间该会话仍被持续 LIST 轮询。原因是 XDRIVE 既没有对端存活检测，也没有背压。

Version: v26.10.17 (`92ccc93`, the newest release and the same commit as current `main`), `network: "xdrive"`, `service: "local"`. XDRIVE is only in the pre-releases since v26.9.30; it is not in v26.3.27. The session logic involved does not depend on the backend, so remote backends behave the same way.

When an XDRIVE client disappears in the middle of a download (process killed, network lost, which is common for mobile clients), the server does not notice:

1. It keeps reading from the target and writes the whole remaining response into the storage. In the repro the client had received 22 MiB of a 256 MiB body; within 20 s after the client was killed the server wrote 246,869,084 bytes in 607 objects.
2. These objects stay until the server-side mux sub-connection ends on its own: about 2.7 min when the target closes the connection after the body, about 13 min with a keep-alive target. Meanwhile the dead session is still polled (about 2 LIST per second).
3. The server logs nothing after the client is gone, even at `debug`.

With a remote backend every abandoned download can upload hundreds of MiB into the storage account, consume API quota and leave the objects there for minutes.

If only the application connection is closed while the client stays alive (curl killed), the server stops writing within about 5 s and the folder is cleaned up, so the problem is specific to the peer disappearing.

| 256 MiB body at 16 MiB/s, `sessionTtlSeconds: 30` | storage at +30 s | +90 s | +180 s | server kept writing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| download completes (control) | 0 B | 0 B | 0 B | no |
| client `kill -9` after ~2 s | 246,869,084 B / 607 objects | same | same | yes, the whole remaining body |
| client `SIGTERM` after ~2 s | 246,394,446 B / 515 objects | same | same | yes |
| curl killed, client alive | 0 B (one `.end`) | 0 B | 0 B | no, stopped within ~5 s |
| client `kill -9`, keep-alive target, watched 900 s | 246,453,796 B | same | same | yes; empty only at ~750–780 s |
| client `kill -9`, target sends `Connection: close` | 246,485,923 B | same | 0 B | yes; empty at ~165 s |

**Cause**

- `Listener.claim` marks the session active (`transport/internet/xdrive/xdrive.go:225`); the mark is removed only in the connection's `onClose` (`xdrive.go:234`). `collect()` skips active sessions (`xdrive.go:267-269`), so the folder of a dead session is not collected while the server-side connection is open.
- That connection is closed only when the inbound handler returns (`app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go:123-127`), i.e. after the server-side mux session ends. issues.title: TUN inbound: Route each new UDP destination, keeping FullCone NAT within a route
issues.body:
The UDP FullCone table (#5509) is keyed by the source only, and only the first packet of a session is routed, so later destinations of that source reuse its outbound. As the TUN never sees a socket close, a port that the OS reuses before the session expires inherits the old route. For example, DNS on a port last used by a direct or blocked flow never reaches the DNS outbound, and a resolver that retries from the same port (mDNSResponder) keeps the stale session alive.

Now a new destination is routed once, with fake IPs judged by their domain and no DNS lookup made. It then joins its source's session for the same rule, or gets a session of its own. Destinations of one rule still share a session, so FullCone is kept within a rule, and a balancer picking another outbound doesn't split it. Routing runs off the goroutine that reads the tun. WireGuard and MASQUE servers are unchanged.

Checked on a real utun on macOS with the system resolver: DNS on a reused port is answered and destinations of one rule leave from one port, while on main the DNS goes nowhere and every destination leaves from the first one. A new destination costs about 2 µs more; established flows and throughput are unchanged.

> ::: warning 循环依赖
任意查询交给内置 DNS 模块处理时，若选中 DNS 服务器的 `address` 不含 `+local`，则到该服务器的连接会交给路由。若 `address` 是域名，路由脚本可能再次调用内置 DNS 解析它。新的查询可能按 DNS 和路由规则顺利完成，也可能经过多个 DNS 服务器和出站，重新依赖尚未完成的解析，形成死循环。

> 其他出站也有另一种成环路径。若代理出站的服务器地址为域名，且 `sockopt.domainStrategy` 非 `AsIs`，出站就会调用内置 DNS 解析该地址。例如，出站 A 依赖 DNS A 的解析结果，而 DNS A 的查询又被送回出站 A，就会形成死循环；也可能先送到出站 B，再因解析 B 的服务器地址而回到 DNS A，形成更长的依赖链。这些出站与 DNS 之间的循环与路由脚本无关，需另行规避，此处不再赘述。

issues.title: XMC finalmask: Bound padding schedules; Fix delay placement; Stop compressing frames
issues.body:
Follow-up to #7402, rebased onto `main` after both #7402 and #7430 merged: this is no longer a stacked draft, the diff is four commits, and it also settles the delay question and the compression side effect that #7402 left behind.

1. **Bound padding schedules and cancel their pauses on Close** (unchanged from the draft). Padding pauses are timers that watch a per-connection `done` channel; a configured schedule is rejected above 256 turns, 64 MiB of turns, or the handshake deadline minus ten seconds of pauses; an explicit empty `paddings` array (or `"noPadding": true`) disables padding, and an absent field keeps the preset.

2. **Pause before a padding turn and never after the last one**. A configured `delay` used to be applied *after* its turn, so the last turn of a schedule paused even though nothing followed it: with `delay: "300"` on the final turn the first proxied packet went out 300 ms later, while both ends otherwise waited for nothing. The pause now leads into the turn it is configured on - a captured gap is written on the turn that follows it - and the last turn is not followed by a pause. Which value each end waits is unchanged and now stated in the proto comment: the side that sends the turn samples `[delay_min, delay_max]`, the peer spends exactly `delay_min` (it waits the minimum, not "at least" it), so a range jitters only the sending side and `delay_min == delay_max` reproduces a captured gap.

3. **State what a configured padding list replaces**. Two decisions only lived in the pull request: a configured list is the complete schedule, so the preset's Play-state join tail runs only with the preset; and a peer cannot be checked for arriving early, because the turns are ordinary Minecraft packets that carry nothing to compare an early arrival against, with the pause bound covering a stalled peer. Both are now next to the code and pinned by a test.

4. **Never compress the frames XMC writes**. After `Set Compression` the writer deflated everything at or above the threshold, which is exactly the padding (zeros, ~300:1) and the proxied bytes (already compressed or encrypted): the padded shape disappeared and the CPU work bought nothing. The writer now always sends the uncompressed variant, which vanilla accepts at any size (`Data Length = 0` is not subject to the threshold check), and the reader still inflates what a real server sends.

#7430 landed while this was open and added a startup reader that drains the peer's padding independently while the local schedule writes. That is why point 3 no longer says the peer's turns stay in the stream for the next reader: they are read and dropped by that reader, while the pause limit still bounds a stalled peer. This branch is rebased onto #7430, and the two changes coexist - the reader drains, and the schedule still spends `delay_min` on the peer's turn. The handshake test that #7430 added now builds its schedule through this branch's `paddingScheduleFromConfig` instead of passing `[]*Padding` to the constructors.

issues.title: Happy Eyeballs: add successDefinition to race until TLS handshake completes
issues.body:
## Motivation

When the server's domain resolves to several IPs, Happy Eyeballs is supposed to pick a working one. In Russia, however, some ISPs (the DPI boxes installed at them) drop the ServerHello for some of these IPs while TCP to them still connects. Which IPs are affected differs from one ISP and region to another and changes over time: an IP that is blocked for one client works for another, so removing it from DNS would only break it for everyone else. Happy Eyeballs today ends the race at the first TCP connection, so it happily picks such an IP, and then the TLS or REALITY handshake can never complete. A retry usually picks the same IP again, because it wins the TCP race again. In this situation the current Happy Eyeballs is of no use at all, even though other IPs of the same domain work fine.

## What this PR adds

A new optional field `successDefinition` in `sockopt.happyEyeballs`:

| Value | The race is won by |
|---|---|
| `tcpConnected` (default) | the first established TCP connection, as before |
| `tlsHandshakeComplete` | the first connection that completes the TLS or REALITY handshake |

```json
"sockopt": {
  "domainStrategy": "UseIP",
  "happyEyeballs": {
    "tryDelayMs": 250,
    "maxConcurrentTry": 4,
    "successDefinition": "tlsHandshakeComplete"
  }
}
```

Without `successDefinition`, or with `tcpConnected`, nothing changes. Without TLS or REALITY, `tlsHandshakeComplete` is the same as `tcpConnected`.

The behaviour follows section 6.1 of Happy Eyeballs v3, which says clients SHOULD wait for the TLS handshake to complete before canceling other attempts: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-happy-happyeyeballs-v3/
Chromium's Happy Eyeballs v3 implementation does the same: a TCP-based attempt runs the TLS handshake inside it and completes only when the handshake does, and an attempt counts as slow (so the next one starts) if TCP and TLS together take longer than the connection attempt delay:
- https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/net/socket/tls_stream_attempt.cc
- https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/net/http/http_stream_pool_attempt.cc

Happy Eyeballs v3 is still a draft, and browsers do not use it by default yet: in Chromium it is behind the `HappyEyeballsV3` feature, which is disabled by default, and Firefox enables it only in Nightly.

## How it works

- The scheduler of `TcpRaceDial` is reused as is (`tryDelayMs`, `maxConcurrentTry`, `prioritizeIPv6`, `interleave`); only the attempt it runs differs. With `tcpConnected` the attempt is the same system dial as before.
- With `tlsHandshakeComplete` every attempt goes through TCP dial to one IP → FinalMask (if any) → the transport's own TLS or REALITY handshake. Only the TCP destination changes from attempt to attempt; masks apply to each attempt separately, exactly as on a normal dial.
- An attempt keeps its `maxConcurrentTry` slot until its handshake ends, and a hanging handshake does not stop the scheduler from starting the next attempt after `tryDelayMs`.
- Losing attempts are stopped by closing their connections. Transports that leave the handshake to the first write (gRPC, and HTTPUpgrade and XHTTP with Go TLS) get it completed inside the race, so a connection is never handshaked twice.
- The race happens under the same conditions as the TCP race in `DialSystem`: `domainStrategy` set, at least two IPs, no `dialerProxy`, non-zero `tryDelayMs` and `maxConcurrentTry`. Otherwise the transport dials exactly as before.

All covered transports now dial through `internet.DialTCPWithHandshake(ctx, dest, streamSettings, handshake)`. `handshake` is a function that wraps the TCP connection with the transport's TLS or REALITY client; it holds the same code the transport used to run right after its own TCP dial.

Transports covered: RAW (TLS, REALITY), WebSocket, HTTPUpgrade, gRPC (TLS, REALITY), XHTTP over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 (TLS, REALITY), MASQUE over HTTP/2. For XHTTP the race runs once per new physical connection. UDP

issues.title: DNS: avoid mutating cache records during cleanup
issues.body:
Built-in DNS cache lookups can race with periodic cleanup. `findRecords` returns a shared `*record` after releasing the cache read lock, and the caller then reads its `A` and `AAAA` fields. Meanwhile, `writeAndShrink` clears those same fields under the write lock; that lock does not protect a lookup that already retained the pointer.

Clean up a new record and publish it under the existing write lock instead of modifying the previously published record. Fully expired entries are still removed, while an unexpired address family is retained. Copies happen during cleanup rather than on every cache lookup.

The tests cover retained lookup records when A, AAAA, both, or neither have expired, and concurrent cached lookups during cleanup.

### Reproduction

Copy `app/dns/cache_controller_test.go` onto base commit `82b5b76b`, then run:

```sh
go test -p=1 -race ./app/dns -run '^TestCacheCleanup' -count=1 -v
```

Before the fix, all three expiry cases modify the retained record and the concurrent test reports a race between `writeAndShrink` and the lookup. With the fix, the same tests pass. The reproduced failure is a data race; a crash or incorrect DNS answer has not been demonstrated.

### Validation

```sh
go test -p=1 -race ./app/dns -run '^TestCacheCleanup' -count=1 -v
go test -p=1 -race ./app/dns -skip '^(TestTCPLocalNameServer|TestDOHNameServer|TestQUICNameServer|TestLocalNameServer)' -count=1
go test -p=1 ./infra/conf -count=1
go run -p=1 ./infra/vformat -pwd . -mode check
git diff --check
```

The DNS suite uses the standard `resources/geoip.dat` fixture. Tests that query external resolvers are excluded from the broader DNS run.

issues.body:
In a diagnostic run of standalone Xray-core, the per-user downlink counter retained 49,152 bytes after `WriteMultiBuffer` failed. The server accepted another 458,752 bytes in successful TLS writes, and the client had yet to read them when it stopped. The stock runs did not measure how many counted bytes came from failed writes.

> Is the per-user downlink counter intended to retain the full buffer length when `WriteMultiBuffer` fails? Could you clarify the counter’s semantics for callers that use it for quota accounting?

## Observed behavior

Standalone Xray-core **26.11.9**, commit `c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2`, on Linux `6.8.0-147-generic` (amd64, stock build Go 1.27.0). A Direct VLESS/raw connection used outer TLS 1.3 and an empty VLESS flow. The HTTPS origin was reached through the SOCKS client and Freedom. Both Xray instances and the origin ran in isolated network namespaces on the same host. A veth egress TBF limited server-to-client traffic to 4 MiB/s. The origin offered 128 MiB at 5 MiB/s.

The genuine StatsService query used `user>>>direct-lab@example.test>>>traffic>>>downlink` without reset. The counter was absent before the first flow on each fresh server and was stable across two post-close queries. A missing initial counter is shown as 0 below.

| Run | Stats before | Stats after | curl HTTP body bytes | VLESS bytes read by client Xray | curl status and time |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| direct-full | 0 | 134399989 | 134217728 | Unmeasured | 0, 33.637729 s |
| direct-cut | 0 | 68890845 | 67108864 | Unmeasured | 18, 16.834965 s |
| diag-cut | 0 | 67719243 | 67108864 | 67211339 | 18, 16.851789 s |

The stock completed run differed from curl by 182,261 bytes. Stats counts the payload inside VLESS, which includes the HTTPS protocol layers toward the origin. curl counts the HTTP body. The completed and cut downloads cover different lengths, so subtracting the full-run overhead from the cut run does not isolate a write failure.

## Diagnostic cut

`XDS_FREEDOM inbound=3 outbound=1 spliceEnabled=true sourceRaw=true writer=*dispatcher.SizeStatWriter`

`XDS_BRANCH readV/buf.Copy reader=*buf.ReadVReader writer=*dispatcher.SizeStatWriter`

The origin-facing Freedom path selected `CopyRawConnIfExist` and fell back to `readV → buf.Copy → SizeStatWriter → BufferedWriter → TLS`. The inbound value `CanSpliceCopy=3` prevented splice. The sum of all 1074 counter increments matched StatsService exactly.

| Diagnostic boundary | Bytes |
|---|---:|
| Final counted buffer, whose `WriteMultiBuffer` returned EPIPE | 65,536 |
| Bytes from that buffer accepted as complete TLS plaintext writes before EPIPE | 16,384 |
| Counted bytes from that buffer without successful TLS writes | **49152** |
| Total VLESS payload accepted as complete TLS writes, after removing two VLESS header bytes | 67670091 |
| Accepted VLESS payload that the client Xray had not read at termination | **458752** |
| Client Xray payload minus curl body, measured at different protocol boundaries | 102475 |

The failed TLS write attempted 8,192 plaintext bytes and returned `n=0, EPIPE`. The other 40,960 bytes in the counted failed buffer were never submitted after that error. At the TCP syscall boundary, 70 ciphertext bytes of the 8,214-byte failed TLS record were accepted. The record was incomplete. Positive TCP write returns for this connection totaled 67855014 ciphertext bytes including outer TLS framing and handshake traffic. That wire total uses a different layer from StatsService.

The three `strace` lines below are separate samples. Their display order does not establish the sequence of a single TLS write.

```text
write(7<TCP:[198.18.198.1:39501->198.18.198.2:36694]>, ""..., 8144) = -1 EPIPE (Broken pipe)
write(7<TCP:[198.18.198.1:39501->198.18.198.2:36694]>, ""..., 8214) = 70

issues.title: Routing: add server-only VMess UUID routes and online user cache
issues.body:
Allow ordinary VMess clients to select declared server-side routes by changing UUID bytes 7 and 8, with only the server upgraded and no account flag required. `userRoute` is the shared routing matcher; `vlessRoute` keeps its existing behavior.

README.md is unchanged in the PR diff.

## Behavior and compatibility

- Generate aliases only for explicit `routing.rules[].userRoute` values applicable to the inbound and user, including existing exact/regexp user matching. Destination-dependent conditions remain routing conditions; Lua-only routing declares no aliases.
- Preserve exact configured UUIDs and the original account's email, policy, statistics and API identity. The experimental account flag and wire extension have been removed completely. Account JSON/protobuf definitions and client encoding match the pre-feature source; no account option or wire field is added.
- Admit connections after normal authenticated header checks. Registration IDs, route generations and pending-change checks reject stale candidates across account/rule changes, including removal and re-addition of the same account object. Closed validators cannot rebuild catalogs.
- Retain identity history during an inbound's lifetime so a removed exact credential cannot become another user's generated alias. Different original route bytes mark the 14-byte identity ambiguous and disable its aliases. Exact credentials remain usable. History is not persisted: independently revocable users and credential rotations must use distinct non-route UUID bytes.
- Align Unicode email removal with the inbound's lowercase index. Retain AuthID replay entries for the full inclusive timestamp-validity interval using 241-second buckets; accepted clock skew and wire encoding remain unchanged. This retains more replay records under sustained traffic.

## Cache and resource bounds

Only authenticated online/recent accounts populate the prepared cache; there are no IP/source-address hints. Idempotent connection leases expire two minutes after the final close. Route changes preserve live leases and idle deadlines without refreshing recency. Search and eviction share one recency list, immutable provider declarations are copied before filtering, and rejected cache growth does not evict unrelated entries.

Per inbound: 64 MiB prepared-key payload, a 128 MiB raw-alias-key limit, and two concurrent alias scans. Oversized live catalogs preserve exact credentials while rejecting aliases. Metadata, replay records and temporary old/new catalog overlap are additional memory. Occupied scan slots can reject further alias handshakes, including hot-cache users; exact credentials bypass those slots.

The amd64 AES-NI/SSE4.1 search accelerator retains all ten AES rounds in a 68-byte schedule and rechecks candidates with the standard-library decoder. Unsupported CPUs, `purego`, and Go FIPS mode select the standard-library fallback. This is not a cryptographic certification or a claim of VLESS-equivalent lookup cost.

## Validation

- VMess, router/command, routing features and configuration tests passed, along with the complete VMess `purego` tests and repository formatting.
- After removing the experimental account flag, all 160 published-binary compatibility cases passed again using clients 1.8.24, 25.12.8 and 26.11.9: 120 ordinary VMess/VLESS cases in both directions, 33 UUID-only/negative/legacy-route cases, and seven byte-identical old-config compilation cases. Coverage includes TCP/UDP, AES-GCM/ChaCha20-Poly1305, Mux, and route values 0/300/65535.
- Known-answer AES plus 4,096 differential decryptions; malformed headers and replay; identity collisions/revocation; concurrent account/rule changes; and 4,000-operation cache lifecycle checks passed. Selected regressions also passed 30 repetitions at each of 1/2/4 CPUs with shuffled order, Go pointer checking, and runtime CPU-feature fallback.
- Windows executable and Linux amd64/arm64 VMess cross-builds passed. The full network scenario package passed

When the UDP idle timer or owner closes a session while `handleInput` is reading, termination cancels the context and interrupts the pipe. The read can return `io.ErrClosedPipe` after the loop's context check, producing an info-level `failed to handle UDP input` message for a local close.

issues.title: XMC finalmask: Switch to native frame padding (breaking); `delay` supports range (receiver waits at least minimal ms)
issues.body:
Follow-up to #6769 (merged in `5d17b872`): completes the remaining `delay` requirement and, per [this reply](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7402#issuecomment-6890345279), switches padding to the more realistic wire format even though that is a breaking change.

## Delay

- `delay` is now a **string**: `"100"` or `"50-150"` (milliseconds). A number written against #6769 no longer parses, so this is a configuration-level breaking change as well.
- The sender waits a uniformly sampled value in `[min, max]` after its turn.
- The receiver waits at least `min` after each turn, including the last one, before the proxy stream starts.
- `config.proto`: `delay` becomes `delay_min` / `delay_max`; negative, reversed and duration-overflowing ranges are rejected at config load.
- `infra/conf`: parses the string delay; tests cover fixed values, ranges and invalid forms.

## Native frame padding (`ea2c7edc`, breaking)

The opaque format wrote a length field that includes its own varint. A vanilla server therefore split the stream one header short and had to take the protocol pipeline over — something a Fabric server mod cannot do without affecting ordinary players.

- One padding chunk becomes one or more configuration-state custom payload frames on `xmc:pad`; the length field now has the vanilla meaning (bytes after the field).
- Chunks above the 32767-byte serverbound payload limit are split; captured 2-byte turns send the smallest possible frame.
- Nothing reads padding any more: it is ordinary traffic that the next reader drops as an unknown packet. Both ends only send and apply the configured pauses.
- The first turn still counts the two Login Acknowledged bytes as its prefix; they are not repeated.
- `maxPacketDataLength` is raised from 32 KiB to 1 MiB (vanilla's clientbound custom payload limit), which a real configuration state can reach with registry data.

**Breaking:** both ends must run this version. No proto field was added for padding; the `paddings` length/direction semantics are unchanged, and `delay` moved from a number to a millisecond string.

Example:

```json
"paddings": [
  {"length": "44", "direction": "c2s", "delay": "0"},
  {"length": "64-128", "direction": "s2c", "delay": "100"},
  {"length": "25", "direction": "c2s", "delay": "50-150"},
  {"length": "32768-49152", "direction": "s2c"}
]
```

Both endpoints should still use the same array and the same `delay` ranges, because that is what reproduces the captured shape. Nothing is compared against the peer's schedule any more, though: the receiver does not consume padding, so a length, direction or turn-count difference can no longer fail or stall the handshake, it only changes what each side sends.

## Scope

Per the cleanup in #6769, this PR does **not** restore the XMC `README.md` / `*_test.go` files deleted in that squash commit. The only new test file is `padding_frames_test.go`, which covers the frame plan/reachability and the source of the padding stream, because the wire format changed here.

## Tests

```text
go test -count=1 ./infra/conf
go test -count=1 ./transport/internet/finalmask/xmc
go build -o /tmp/xray-core-build ./main
go run ./infra/vformat -pwd . -mode check
go run ./infra/vprotogen -pwd . -mode check
```

## Validation fix

A legacy password longer than 113 bytes is now rejected when the configuration is built (`035c45de`), instead of being accepted and then failing every handshake: the verify token plus the password must fit one RSA-1024 PKCS#1 v1.5 block (128-11 bytes), so `rsa.EncryptPKCS1v15` was failing on the client and the server could not decrypt it either.

```text
go test -count=1 ./infra/conf ./transport/internet/finalmask/xmc
```

issues.title: Feature Request: Add udp+local:// DNS scheme (plain UDP local mode)
issues.body:
# Feature Request: Add `udp+local://` DNS scheme (plain UDP local mode)

## Summary

Xray's DNS configuration supports `+local` variants for HTTPS, h2c, QUIC and TCP, but there is **no `udp+local` scheme** for plain UDP DNS in local mode. This means there is currently **no way to send plain UDP DNS queries to a local resolver while bypassing the routing/dispatcher stack**.

## Current state

`app/dns/nameserver.go`, `NewServer()` switch (main branch):

```go
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "https"):      // DoH remote
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "h2c"):        // DoH h2c remote
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "https+local"): // DoH local
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "h2c+local"):   // DoH h2c local
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "quic+local"):  // DoQ local
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "tcp"):         // TCP remote
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "tcp+local"):   // TCP local
case strings.EqualFold(u.String(), "fakedns"):
```

Every protocol except plain UDP has a `+local` form. Plain UDP falls through to the default branch:

```go
if dest.Network == net.Network_UDP {
    return NewClassicNameServer(dest, dispatcher, ...)
}
```

Note that `NewClassicNameServer` receives the `dispatcher`, so plain UDP **always goes through the routing stack** — there is no way to bypass it.

## Why this matters (measured data)

For a local resolver (e.g. smartdns on `127.0.0.1`), bypassing the dispatcher matters. Measured on a local resolver over loopback, one A + one AAAA query for the same domain:

| Path | p50 | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `tcp+local://` (current workaround) | ~810µs | 2 TCP handshakes + 2 closes |
| `tcp+local://` pipelined on 1 conn | ~680µs | would need connection pooling, not implemented |
| **plain UDP, 2 packets sent in parallel** | **~376µs** | no handshake, no teardown |

The UDP path is ~2x faster than the current `tcp+local` workaround because it avoids TCP handshake/teardown entirely. Pairing responses by DNS ID worked in 200/200 trials with zero mismatch.

For users running a local caching resolver, this overhead is paid on every cache-miss lookup.

## Secondary issue: port parsing for bare `udp://` schemes

Related bug found while investigating. With:

```json
"dns": { "servers": ["udp://127.0.0.1:5353"] }
```

xray logs:

```
DNS: created UDP client initialized for udp://127.0.0.1:5353:53
```

The port becomes `5353:53` — the `:5353` is swallowed into the address (as a domain string) and then a default `:53` is appended by:

```go
// app/dns/nameserver_udp.go:41
if address.Port == 0 {
    address.Port = net.Port(53)
}
```

This is because `infra/conf/dns.go` builds the endpoint with `Address` and `Port` as separate fields, and `Address.Build()` calls `net.ParseAddress()` on the whole string including `:5353`, while `Port` stays 0.

Attempting `udp://127.0.0.1` (no port) resolves to `udp://127.0.0.1:53`, which happens to work, but the scheme is still parsed as a domain so the connection fails with:

```
failed to open connection to udp:udp://127.0.0.1:53
> too many colons in address
```

Contrast with `tcp+local`, which parses correctly because it uses `url.Hostname()` and `url.Port()` separately (`app/dns/nameserver_tcp.go:75-81`).

## Proposed change

Add a `udp+local` case that mirrors `tcp+local` — parse host/port via `url.Hostname()` / `url.Port()` and pass `nil` as the dispatcher:

```go
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "udp+local"): // DNS-over-UDP Local mode
    return NewUDPNameServer(u, nil, disableCache, serveStale, serveExpiredTTL, clientIP), nil
```

Where the new constructor resolves the destination the same way `baseTCPNameServer` does:

```go
port := net.Port(53)
if url.Port() != "" {
    if port, err = net.PortFromString(url.Port()); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
}
dest := net.UDPDestination(net.ParseAddress(url.Hostname()), port)
```

This would also give users a documented way to hit a local resolver on a non-53 port without the address-swallowing bug.

Fixes https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/issues/7443

The reader and the writer of one Vision connection run in different goroutines and both call `XtlsFilterTls` on the shared `*TrafficState`, so `NumberOfPacketToFilter`, `IsTLS`, `IsTLS12orAbove`, `Cipher`, `RemainingServerHello` and `EnableXtls` were read and written without synchronization.

issues.body:
# XHTTP: packet-down in stream-down with downlink keep-alive

Follows RPRX's packet-down design in https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/6755#issuecomment-5720463978, which was written while closing the earlier downlink-resume attempt (#6755). That attempt was rejected because "restore connection" is too complex, with latency, ACK and so on. This one does not attempt connection restoration at all. No reconnection, no state machine, nothing to tune: each stream-down GET stays a single request; if the GET dies, the connection dies the ordinary way.

## Problem (from #4846)

CDNs kill a stream-down GET on body inactivity. This matters during uploads: with packet-up the uplink posts keep flowing, but the downlink proxy payload only arrives while the origin sends, so during a pure upload the GET idles and gets cut. Same story for any target that goes quiet for a while after responding.

## What this PR adds

When enabled on both ends, the stream-down response body is cut into packet-down frames with the five elements from the design comment:

- omittable session id excerpt: first 8 bytes of the session id, present on data and keep-alive frames (absent in stream-one where the session id is empty)
- omittable packet seq: uint64, counting data/keep-alive frames per stream-down GET
- mandatory type: data or padding
- mandatory length: uint16
- payload

Use today is the first one from the design comment: downlink keep-alive. While the downlink has been idle for a whole period, the server writes a padding frame (base62, in the spirit of tokenish x-padding) instead of staying silent. Everything the dispatcher sends rides in data frames, which is what lets the client tell padding apart from payload safely; the seq keeps the format ready for the future uses listed in the design comment (retransmission, multi-path-down) without another wire change.

h1, h2 and h3 are covered, since the framers sit on the body, not on a specific transport. stream-one gets the same treatment on its single response body. Browser dialer is out of scope for now: it has no place to read the response header that confirms the framing.

## Negotiation

Strictly opt-in and per request, so old servers are unaffected and nothing breaks behind middleboxes:

1. client config has packetDown: XHTTP stream requests not used as pure uplink (stream-down GET, stream-one request) carry X-Packet-Down: 1
2. server has packetDown configured and sees the marker: it answers with X-Packet-Down: 1 on the response, and frames; without the confirmed header the client never parses frames
3. any other combination: byte-identical wire format as today

## Config

```jsonc
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/sh",
  "packetDown": {              // absent = disabled, as today
    "keepAlive": true,
    "keepAlivePeriod": "10-30",  // seconds; padded when inactive this long. defaults to 10-30
    "keepAliveLength": "24-64"   // padding size. defaults to 24-64
  }
}
```

Server side is the same block in the inbound; the server only honors the feature when the client asks.

## Not in this PR (deliberately)

- obfs of the frames (later, per the design comment)
- retransmission, multi-path-down, same-packet racing, ACK: the format carries seq and the session excerpt, but none of the machinery, exactly like packet-up carries seq today without using it
- nothing about #4846's larger downlink freeze problem (the 15-20 KB per TCP connection cut): this only discards the CDN idle timer, it does not split data across connections

- packet_down_test.go: frame round trip (with/without excerpt, with/without seq), byte-stream shaped like a socket, splitting payloads larger than one frame, padding skipped, malformed frame rejected, keep-alive written when idle, keep-alive suppressed while active, config normalization
- splithttp_test.go: full listen/dial round trip with packet-down on both end (100 KiB), and the fallback case with the client setting present but the server without one
- infra/conf: JSON un

issues.title: Feature request: configurable TLS fingerprint selection with weights and an explicit allowlist
issues.body:
As one of many VPN services using Xray, we’d find it useful to configure multiple TLS fingerprints, assign each a percentage (chance of choosing specific fingerprint on connection, analogous to `random`), and explicitly exclude fingerprints that do not work in our target networks. The core would select a fingerprint once per new connection according to those weights.

For example: **Firefox 9%, Chrome 70%, Edge 12%, Safari 9%**, with `ios`, `android`, and `chrome-133` excluded.

In our experience, Russian DPI blocks connections using those three fingerprints in some cases. Unrestricted random selection is therefore risky: individual connections may fail simply because an incompatible fingerprint was selected.

We previously used Firefox because it worked well in our environment. However, what works today may change, and having 100% of connections share the same normalized TLS fingerprint could itself help TSPU identify VPN traffic.

Weighted selection would reduce this uniformity, while explicit control over the allowed fingerprints would help preserve reliability. This would not make VPN traffic indistinguishable from browsers, but it would give operators a practical way to manage that tradeoff.

issues.title: XHTTP/3: drain connections filled by long-lived streams
issues.body:
Fixes #7397.

## Reproduction

`TestH3PacketUpAtStreamLimit` runs an XHTTP/3 client and echo server on loopback. The server allows two bidirectional QUIC streams and the client uses `xmux.maxConnections: 1`. The first session receives a greeting and echoes one byte. A second session then receives its greeting on the same QUIC connection, confirming that the server has accepted both long-lived download requests.

On `82b5b76b`, the next upload from the **first** session needs a third request stream. Both available streams are still carrying downloads, so the echo times out after three seconds. To reproduce, copy `transport/internet/splithttp/packet_up_h3_test.go` from this PR into the same directory on that commit and run:

```sh
go test -count=1 -run '^TestH3PacketUpAtStreamLimit$' ./transport/internet/splithttp
```

The failing assertion is `first session after second download: timed out`.

## Why GOAWAY preserves the sessions

On listeners that allow packet-up, the server counts long-lived requests on each QUIC connection. When they occupy every bidirectional stream, it starts graceful HTTP/3 shutdown for that connection. GOAWAY tells the client to send new requests elsewhere while the server continues serving the accepted downloads. The next upload can use a replacement connection and its XHTTP session ID still routes it to the original session. The draining and replacement connections can coexist, each respecting the configured stream limit. [RFC 9114 §5.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9114.html#section-5.2)

## Verification

With `a327c3d9`, both original sessions echoed data after the second download opened. A third session echoed data on a different connection, as checked by the peer address at the server. The listener also shut down with both connections in use.

```sh
go test -race -count=50 -run '^TestH3PacketUpAtStreamLimit$' ./transport/internet/splithttp
go test -race -count=1 ./transport/internet/splithttp
```

Both commands passed. Separate runs also passed with a one-stream limit in auto mode and with the client implementation from the base commit against the patched server. The CLI build and repository format check passed. Package vet reported the same warnings on both commits.

issues.title: XDRIVE: delete S3 objects before their parent directories
issues.body:
Fixes #7428.

XDRIVE's S3 cleanup deletes the session key before listing its children. On a backend that rejects deletion of nonempty directories, the first DELETE returns HTTP 412 and cleanup stops. This change collects the keys under the session prefix across all list pages and deletes them in reverse lexicographic order. Each child is deleted before its directory marker, and the session key is deleted last. Cleanup holds one key string per listed object in memory.

## Reproduction

`TestS3DeleteNonemptyDirectory` uses the production S3 client against a local HTTP test server. The server returns 412 for a DELETE while the directory has children. It lists the `abc/up/` marker on the first page and its segment on the second. After deleting session `abc`, the test checks that the only remaining key belongs to the neighboring session `abcd`.

To reproduce on the base commit, run these commands from the PR checkout. They copy the new test into a temporary copy of the original source tree.

```sh
before=$(mktemp -d)

issues.title: XMC finalmask: Prevent deadlock during bidirectional startup padding
issues.body:
XMC startup padding can deadlock after #7402 when both directions exceed the connection buffers. Both endpoints write their entire local schedule before starting the packet reader, so neither drains the peer's padding and both writes eventually time out.

Drain incoming `xmc:pad` packets while sending startup padding. Retain the first non-padding packet and then hand reading back to the packet stream, buffering at most one packet. The padding wire format and configured pauses are preserved. A startup write failure closes the connection to release the pending reader.

For example, this valid schedule can stall both endpoints:

```json
"paddings": [
  {"direction": "c2s", "length": "8388608"},
  {"direction": "s2c", "length": "8388608"}
]
```

The regression test exercises the full encrypted handshake over `net.Pipe` with 64 KiB turns and TCP with 8 MiB turns and constrained socket buffers, followed by proxy data in both directions. The pipe handshake failed on both endpoints before the fix. Reader tests cover preserving following packets, read errors, empty reads, and connection closure.

Checked the 57 currently open PRs: only #7423 and #7416 modify XMC. #7423 handles schedule bounds/cancellation and #7416 handles authentication; neither adds concurrent padding reads.

Validation passed:

```text
go test -p=1 ./transport/internet/finalmask/... ./infra/conf -count=1
go test -p=1 -race ./transport/internet/finalmask/xmc -count=1
go run -p=1 ./infra/vformat -pwd . -mode check
```

issues.title: XTLS Vision: Fix panic and silent data loss on oversized buffers
issues.body:
### Problem

`ReshapeMultiBuffer` splits an oversized buffer once and writes the whole remainder into a single new buffer, discarding the `ErrBufferFull` that `Write` returns:

```go
buffer2 := buf.New()
buffer2.Write(buffer1.BytesFrom(index))
```

Buffers longer than `buf.Size` reach it, because `buf.NewExisted` only enforces a minimum capacity and the gRPC transport wraps hunks of arbitrary size with it (`grpc/encoding/hunkconn.go:97`, `multiconn.go:78`). The remainder is truncated to exactly `buf.Size`, so `XtlsPadding` computes `paddingLen = buf.Size - 21 - buf.Size = -21` and `Buffer.Extend` slices `b.v[8192:8171]`, which panics and takes down the process. With the default split point of `buf.Size/2` the threshold is 12288 bytes.

### Fix

Copy the remainder out in chunks of at most `buf.Size-21`, the largest content `XtlsPadding` can fit, until nothing is left. Buffers up to `buf.Size` keep their previous two-piece shape, so normal traffic is unaffected.

### Verification

On unmodified `main` (`f781c687`), a 12288-byte buffer panics with `slice bounds out of range [8192:8171]`. With this change, inputs of 8213 / 12288 / 20000 / 65535 bytes produce 2 / 3 / 3 / 9 buffers, every byte preserved and no piece above `buf.Size-21`. For inputs up to `buf.Size` the output shape is unchanged across the range of split points.

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go run ./infra/vformat -mode check` and `go test ./...` are clean; the three geodata-dependent packages fail identically on unmodified `main` here because `geoip.dat` / `geosite.dat` are absent locally.

I reproduced this at the function level with the same `buf.NewExisted` constructor the gRPC transport uses, not end-to-end through a live gRPC inbound.

### On scope

Kept inside `ReshapeMultiBuffer`. Rejecting `n < 0` in `Buffer.Extend` would swap one panic for another without addressing the truncation, and stopping `buf.NewExisted` from returning oversized buffers looks intended. Happy to take whichever shape you prefer.

Fixes #7369. Same panic signature as #2651, #5961 and #6072.

issues.title: FakeDNS: avoid repeated allocation scans with a fixed-width cursor
issues.body:
FakeDNS currently chooses a starting address from the current millisecond on every cache miss. During a burst of queries for new domains, successive allocations repeatedly scan the same occupied addresses. This work happens under the holder mutex, so it also delays other queries using that holder, even when the pool has plenty of free addresses.

Keep an allocation cursor between queries instead. This removes the repeated scans in that workload and fixes address-width loss in the same allocation path.

## What changes

- Store a `netip.Addr` cursor per holder, initialize it once at a random address inside the configured pool, and continue from the previous allocation.
- Advance past occupied addresses and wrap at the pool boundary, including overflow at the end of the IPv4 or IPv6 address space.
- Preserve the existing allocation lock, LRU eviction and reverse-lookup behavior. Integer capacity validation requires a positive LRU size smaller than the pool, leaving a free address available before insertion.

The current `big.Int.Bytes()` conversion drops leading zero bytes. On unmodified upstream `f781c687`, a local reproduction returned a nil address for `0.1.0.0/16` and an IPv4 address for the IPv6 pool `::100:0/112`. Fixed-width addresses preserve the configured family and make these pools return valid, in-pool answers.

## Measured effect

A local microbenchmark allocates the same 4,096 distinct names in a fresh default IPv4 holder on each iteration. Three samples, five iterations per sample, on Windows amd64 with Go 1.27.3 and an Intel Core i5-11600K:

| Per 4,096-name burst | Upstream | This change |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Time | 861–956 ms | 1.70–3.68 ms |
| Allocations | 21.1–21.8 million | About 39,800 |

These measurements cover the allocator workload, not end-to-end proxy throughput. Occupied addresses still require probing; this does not make every allocation constant-time.

## Validation

- Existing FakeDNS and cache package tests passed.
- Additional local checks compared 493,568 operations with an independent LRU model, covering every starting address and valid cache capacity in twelve small IPv4/IPv6 pools. These included leading-zero addresses, address-space limits and IPv4-mapped IPv6 notation.
- 262,144 concurrent forward/reverse lookup pairs passed, with final uniqueness checks.
- A built Xray process answered repeated A and AAAA queries over loopback using an ordinary FakeDNS configuration.
- Focused regressions also ran on Windows 386; the FakeDNS tests compiled for Linux amd64 and macOS arm64. The Go race detector was not run.

Only `app/dns/fakedns/fake.go` changes. The cursor lasts for the holder's lifetime; it does not persist mappings across core restarts or change the existing consequences of LRU eviction for applications retaining old fake addresses.

comments.body:
Thank you @anonymousmeower, that explains it. We do have a gRPC inbound on this relay (7 clients, roughly a third of all connections), and the bursts line up with a threshold like 12288.

I reproduced it independently on v25.12.8 (`81f8f39`) with a small test: a 12288-byte buffer created with `buf.NewExisted` goes through `ReshapeMultiBuffer`, the second piece is exactly 8192 bytes, and `XtlsPadding` then computes `paddingLen = -21`. Agreed that clamping `paddingLen` is the wrong fix (it just trades a crash for truncation), the split has to be done properly.

This is what we run now on the production relay, in case it is useful as a starting point (it only changes the oversize path; buffers whose remainder fits are split exactly as before):

```go
tail := buffer1.BytesFrom(index)
var pieces []*buf.Buffer
for len(tail) > 0 {
	n := len(tail)
	if n > buf.Size-21 {
		n = buf.Size - 21
	}
	piece := buf.New()
	piece.Write(tail[:n])
	pieces = append(pieces, piece)
	tail = tail[n:]
}
buffer1.Resize(0, index)
mb2 = append(mb2, buffer1)
for _, piece := range pieces {
	mb2 = append(mb2, piece)
}
```

A test with sizes 8171 / 8192 / 8213 / 12288 / 16384 / 20000 / 40000 (with and without a TLS application-data header) passes: every piece is <= `buf.Size-21`, the concatenation equals the input, and `XtlsPadding` does not panic on any piece. The same test fails on the unpatched code at 12288. Interop with sing-box and Xray 24/25/26 clients over Reality, XHTTP and gRPC is unchanged in our matrix. We will report back after a few days of real traffic (the relay was crashing about 100 times a day before).

comments.issue_title: XMC finalmask: Bound padding schedules; Fix delay placement; Stop compressing frames
comments.body:
@RPRX 结论先说：MC 协议本身没有 padding，也没有任何"延迟/时序"字段；真机上 join 收尾的最后一个包之后也没有停顿——同一个 tick 里就会发 `Client Tick End`，之后每 50 ms 一个。所以"the last one 之后需不需要 delay"在真机上对应的是"下一个包在同一个 tick 内到"，而不是"停一下"。

**MC 协议到底是什么**

1. 帧：一条 TCP 连接上就是 VarInt 长度分帧，`长度 | 包体`；包体是 `packet id + 字段`。`Set Compression` 之后包体前面多一个 `data length`：`data length = 0` 表示未压缩，非 0 才走 zlib。vanilla 服务端接受超过 threshold 的未压缩包，只拒绝小于 threshold 的压缩包（这个 PR 第 4 点靠的就是它）。帧上限 2^21-1；serverbound custom payload 数据 ≤ 32767 B，clientbound ≤ 1 MiB。
2. 状态机：Handshaking → Status / Login → Configuration → Play。登录阶段可选 RSA + AES-CFB8；之后整条流（包括长度字段）都是密文，路径上的观察者只看得到"什么时候、多少字节"。
3. 协议里唯一和时间有关的规则是 keep-alive：服务端每 1–15 s 发一次，客户端 15 s 不回被踢，20 s 收不到就 Timed out。除此之外没有节流、没有填充、没有时序协商。
4. 客户端的"节奏"是 20 Hz 游戏循环（50 ms/tick）：一个 tick 里产生的包各自 write+flush，Nagle 关掉，所以 wire 上的间隔基本就是 tick。

**"最后一个包之后"在真机上**

查了 26.1 官方客户端（反编译），`Minecraft.tick()` 里的顺序是：

- `gameMode.tick()` → `Connection.tick()` → `ClientPacketListener.tick()` → `notifyPlayerLoaded()`：加载地形结束时发 `Player Loaded`；
- `level.tickEntities()`：玩家第一次 tick（wiki 说"第一次玩家 tick 发生在这个包和下一个 Client Tick End 之间"就是这里）；
- `connection.send(ServerboundClientTickEndPacket.INSTANCE)`：`Client Tick End`，无字段，2 字节帧。

所以 `Player Loaded` 和下一个 `Client Tick End` 在同一个 tick 内，间隔就是该 tick 剩下的工作量（通常几 ms），然后才是 50 ms 网格。capture 看起来"停在最后"，是因为 schedule 只建模到 player_loaded，后面交给隧道了；真机在后面是持续的心跳。

**对 #7423**

- "pause 前移到 turn 上、最后一个 turn 之后不暂停"是对的：captured gap 属于"下一个包什么时候来"，不属于"上一个包之后停多久"；最后一个 turn 后面没有下一个 turn，这个 pause 没有地方放。
- 硬加一个尾部 delay 反而会造出真机没有的空洞：真机那个位置只有 tick 的剩余时间（几 ms）。
- join 收尾之后真正缺的不是 delay，而是 20 Hz 心跳；而 XMC 停在 Configuration，这个状态里 vanilla 客户端只有回应、没有 tick 包，所以它也不是 padding schedule 能补的，属于另一个设计问题。

结论：这个 PR 不需要为"最后一个之后的 delay"改模型。


参考：[Packets#Packet_format](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Java_Edition_protocol/Packets#Packet_format)、[FAQ 登录序列](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Java_Edition_protocol/FAQ#What's_the_normal_login_sequence_for_a_client?)、[Player Loaded](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Java_Edition_protocol/Packets#Player_Loaded)、[Keep Alive](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Java_Edition_protocol/Packets#Keep_Alive_(clientbound))

comments.body:
Additional end-to-end observation: cancelling HTTP requests while the VPN client stayed running led to the same quota deduction as a full download in a controlled WaterWall → Xray/XMPlus test.

Each run requested 40 HTTPS objects of 2 MiB each (two parallel requests per simulated video, 20 videos). The full run completed all 40. The cancellation run cancelled each pair 300 ms after both HTTP requests were sent, without stopping the VPN client. The controlled origin completed its writes for all 40 objects in both runs.

| Run | Reported downlink (bytes) | VLESS payload read by client (bytes) | Reported uplink (bytes) | Actual quota deduction (bytes) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Full | 84,080,320 | 84,080,320 | 29,110 | 84,109,430 |
| Cancelled | 84,080,320 | 6,565,384 | 29,110 | 84,109,430 |

The cancelled run's downlink-to-client gap was **77,514,936 bytes (73.92 MiB)**. At a traffic multiplier of 1, the new panel traffic rows reconciled exactly with the actual quota decrease. This experiment measures the total gap between server reporting and client reads. It did not isolate failed writes from bytes accepted by intermediate buffers. The impact on customers who reported unexpected quota use is still unknown.

comments.issue_title: panic: slice bounds out of range [8192:8171] in XtlsPadding (VLESS outbound, Reality + Vision), recurring ~6x/hour on 25.6.8 / 25.9.5 / 25.12.8
comments.body:
The path is `buf.NewExisted`: it only enforces a *minimum* capacity, so it returns buffers longer than `buf.Size` — and the gRPC transport wraps hunks of arbitrary size with it (`grpc/encoding/hunkconn.go:97`, `multiconn.go:78`). You have a gRPC inbound.

`ReshapeMultiBuffer` splits such a buffer once and writes the whole remainder into one new buffer, discarding the `ErrBufferFull` from `Write`:

```go
buffer2 := buf.New()
buffer2.Write(buffer1.BytesFrom(index))
```

With no TLS record header in range, `index` is `buf.Size/2` = 4096, so a 12288-byte buffer leaves a remainder of exactly 8192: `buffer2.Len() == buf.Size`, and above that size the surplus is dropped with the error. `XtlsPadding` then gets `paddingLen = 8192 - 21 - 8192 = -21`, and `Extend(-21)` slices `b.v[8192:8171]`.

Reproduced on current main (`f781c687`): 8213 bytes is fine, 12288 panics with your exact string. So the threshold is 12288 = 4096 + 8192, which fits a clustered few-per-hour rate rather than every connection.

On the hardening you suggested: clamping `paddingLen` at 0 stops the crash but keeps the truncation — 7712 of 20000 bytes dropped — trading a crash for stream corruption. The fix belongs in `ReshapeMultiBuffer`, which should keep splitting until the remainder fits.

comments.issue_title: upgrade klauspost/compress to fix (CVE-2026-116591)
comments.body:
> ~是仅 panic 而不会通过认证吧~

Yes, you're correct — it only causes a panic and does **not** bypass authentication.

After reviewing the code and running tests, here's the precise breakdown:

**Root cause — `proxy/socks/protocol.go` line 206:**

```go
// If s.config.Address is set to a domain (e.g. "localhost" or "example.com"),
// AsAddress() returns a domainAddress, and calling .IP() on it panics.
udpHub, err := internet.ListenSystemPacket(
    context.Background(),
    &net.UDPAddr{IP: responseAddress.IP(), Port: 0},  // 💥 panic here
    nil,
)
```

This is because `domainAddress.IP()` in `common/net/address.go` unconditionally panics:

```go
func (domainAddress) IP() net.IP {
    panic("Calling IP() on a DomainAddress.")
}
```

**Why it is NOT an authentication bypass:**

The panic occurs at line 206, which is reached only *after* `auth5()` completes successfully at line 148. An unauthenticated or wrongly-authenticated client is rejected before the panic site is ever reached (confirmed by testing all three scenarios: no-auth client, wrong-password client, and no-auth server).

**Trigger conditions:**

The vulnerable path requires the server operator to have explicitly set `address` to a domain name (e.g. `"localhost"`) in the SOCKS inbound config. A remote attacker has no control over `responseAddress` — it comes from `s.config.Address` (server config), not from client input. The client only needs to send a `UDP ASSOCIATE` command to trigger the crash once the misconfiguration is in place.

**Impact:** This is a **misconfiguration-induced crash** (DoS), not a security vulnerability. If `address` is left empty (default) or set to a valid IP, the panic never occurs.

issues.body:
Приветствую.

Прежде всего — спасибо за клиент и за то, что проект открыт: разбираться по исходникам и по вашим ответам в обращениях можно, и это очень помогает.

Пишу о поведении, которое мешает в работе, и постараюсь изложить его так, чтобы вам было меньше работы: только наблюдения, журналы и то, что я уже проверил сам.

**Что происходит**

Нажимаю "Отключить". В части случаев всё проходит как надо: значок остаётся в трее, служба убирает маршруты. В остальных случаях окно и значок исчезают — программа завершается, а служба продолжает работать. Подключение при этом всегда проходит нормально.

Частота. За шесть циклов "подключить — отключить" подряд: четыре завершения. После того как в раздельное туннелирование по приложениям были добавлены две программы, из двух циклов завершился один. Похоже, дело не в настройках, а в моменте — то есть в гонке.

**Обстановка**

- Windows 11 IoT Enterprise LTSC, 10.0.26100 (24H2), x64.
- AmneziaVPN 5.1.0.6 (файл `C:\Program Files\AmneziaVPN\AmneziaVPN.exe`), Qt 6.11.1 (`Qt6RemoteObjects.dll` 6.11.1.0).
- Драйвер `mullvad-split-tunnel.sys` 1.2.5.0, служба `AmneziaVPNSplitTunnel`.
- Протокол VLESS (XRay) с `tun2socks.exe`.
- Настройки: раздельное туннелирование по сайтам включено; по приложениям включено, в списке две записи (`max.exe`, `max-service.exe`); kill switch выключен; собственный DNS Amnezia выключен; автозапуск с ключом `--autostart`, запуск свёрнутым.
- Клиент запущен обычным путём (автозапуск и оболочка рабочего стола), внешним менеджером процессов не управляется.

**Что видно в журнале службы**

Удачный цикл — служба успевает всё сделать, канал жив:

```
[16:48:11.724Z] Xray::stopXray()
[16:48:13.443Z] IpcServerProcess errorOccurred  QProcess::Crashed
[16:48:13.457Z] RouterWin::clearSavedRoutes forward rows size: 8
[16:48:13.460Z] Router::clearSavedRoutes : removed routes: 4 of 8
```

Неудачный цикл — те же шаги, но после остановки `tun2socks` служба замолкает, уборки маршрутов нет:

```
[16:48:53.761Z] Xray::stopXray()
[16:48:55.561Z] IpcServerProcess errorOccurred  QProcess::Crashed
```

Ранний неудачный цикл, где ошибка канала видна явно:

```
[15:40:11.985Z] Xray::stopXray()
[15:40:12.424Z] QWindowsPipeWriter: write failed. (Канал был закрыт.)
[15:40:13.729Z] IpcServerProcess errorOccurred  QProcess::Crashed
```

Между командой отключения и обрывом канала проходит от 0.4 до 1.7 секунды. В удачных циклах `clearSavedRoutes` успевает выполниться, в неудачных — нет.

issues.title: feat(split-tunneling): wildcard site entries, resolved by observing DNS
issues.body:
Fixes #1607.

## Why a wildcard cannot simply be added to the list

Site split tunnelling selects by destination address, because that is all a
routing table has. The addresses behind `*.discord.gg` are not knowable when the
entry is typed, and a CDN keeps changing them, so there is nothing to install.
Entering a domain already works by resolving it once and storing the answer, but
a wildcard cannot be resolved at all: there is no query that returns every name
below a label.

The only place where the name still exists is the DNS exchange itself. This
change puts a forwarder where the system already sends its queries, relays them
to the real resolvers, and installs an exclusion route for the addresses of the
answers whose name matches a pattern, while the answer is still on its way back
to the application.

## What is in it

Four commits, each one reviewable on its own:

1. **The forwarder, the shared definition of a wildcard, and the route table.**
   No caller yet.
2. **The UI and configuration path**: storing a pattern, and carrying it to the
   daemon.
3. **The daemon and the platform work**: installing, permitting and withdrawing
   what is learned.
4. **Fixes from the review** below: reserved addresses, the server switch, route
   lifetime, per-pattern budgets, dedicated firewall anchors on Linux and macOS,
   UDP/TCP failover in the forwarder, client-side gating and log privacy.

### Trusting an answer

What the forwarder reports becomes a route in a privileged daemon, so a reply is
believed only when all of this holds: it arrived from the resolver the query was
sent to, on a socket connected to it; the transaction id and the question match
the query; the response bit is set, the opcode is zero, there is no error, and
the answer is not truncated. Addresses are taken only from records whose owner is
the queried name or a name reached from it through the CNAMEs of that same
message, and each address inherits the shortest TTL along that path. Everything
else is handed to the application untouched and reported to nobody.

Because the forwarder replaces the system's resolver list, it does the
failover the system would otherwise do. A UDP query is retransmitted across
the configured resolvers (1 s per attempt, 5 s in total, a single resolver
being retried), a late answer to an earlier attempt is still accepted, and the
resolver that answered last is tried first. A TCP resolver that closes with
queries outstanding is reconnected and the queries resent. Only when the budget
runs out is the query answered with SERVFAIL, rather than left to time out.

Queries are served from the machine itself and from directly attached
subnets of other interfaces (local containers). Peers reaching the address
over the tunnel are refused, because what the forwarder learns becomes a
route.

### Names are never flattened

A DNS label may legally contain a dot. Names coming off the wire are kept as a
list of labels and compared label by label, so a single label whose bytes read
`x.example.com` does not pass for a name below `example.com`. Patterns are stored
canonically: lower case, no trailing dot, the base put through IDNA, and a path,
white space or an empty label refused at the point of entry. `*.пример.рф` is
stored as `*.xn--e1afmkfd.xn--p1ai`, which is the form that actually arrives.

### How long a learned route lives

A learned route lasts for the session. It is not withdrawn on a timer: an open
connection keeps using the address after the TTL, and the system resolver can
serve the record from its cache for as long as the TTL says. Once the full TTL
plus an hour has passed (on a monotonic clock), the entry is stale. A stale
entry is evicted, least recently seen first, only when its pattern or the
table is full. All learned routes are withdrawn on disconnect, on a server
switch to a different configuration, and when the pattern list changes.

Main window opens.

fix(windows): prevent large split-tunnel lists from stalling connections
issues.body:
Large split-tunnel lists on Windows repeatedly read the growing routing table and queue a full rescan for each route-change notification. This can leave the client waiting for a handshake after the routes have already been installed.

Batch exclusion additions and removals using one routing-table snapshot per address family. Temporarily unsubscribe from route notifications during bulk updates and rescans, and use an atomic pending flag to queue at most one rescan. Preserve duplicate-prefix reference counts and parse CIDR exclusions correctly when switching servers. Also fix the inverted success check when refreshing captured routes after exclusions are removed.

Platforms without a batch implementation retain the existing per-prefix fallback.

Validation:

- Built the Windows x64 Release client and service with Qt 6.10 and MSVC 19.50, and generated an IFW installer. Checked the packaged EXE/DLL imports: no unresolved dependencies.
- A temporary native regression harness using the production daemon and route-monitor code with mocked Windows routing APIs passed 2/2 CTest tests. The original code performed 512 full rescans for 512 notifications; the fix coalesced 12,902 notifications into one rescan and installed a 12,902-prefix list with one IPv4 table read.
- Covered mixed IPv4/IPv6 batches, concurrent callbacks, gateway changes, duplicate references, CIDR server switches, handshake timer delivery, disconnect/reconnect, capture refresh, and snapshot-failure recovery.

Manual validation: the rebuilt Windows client and service were tested on a self-hosted server with the imported 12,902-prefix split-tunnel list; the VPN connection was verified successfully.

Related: #3425, #3114, #2516.

- the Kill Switch WFP rules permit traffic only through the VPN interface (and appear to whitelist `AmneziaVPN.exe`);

## Problem
Installing or reconfiguring a self-hosted MTProxy or Telemt service can put proxy access credentials in the application's diagnostic log when logging is enabled. Exporting the log archive can then disclose those credentials to its recipient.

The configure scripts intentionally return machine-readable credentials. ```

Note `Permit (out) IPv4 Traffic of: AmneziaVPN-service` and the explicit permit for `<server-ip>/32`: the service process **is** allowed and the endpoint is excluded before the handshake. In this run Kill Switch did not block the handshake, and NCSI reported `ActiveHttpProbeSucceeded` on the tunnel adapter ~4 s later.

### Revised assessment

The earlier failures (17:19, 17:52, 17:59) are most consistent with the tunnel itself failing to establish (server/DPI transient) while Kill Switch did what it is designed to do: fail closed. The remaining issues are about recovery and diagnostics:

1. **No rollback/timeout when the tunnel fails**: the client stays in "Connecting" indefinitely and all DNS/Internet remains blocked until the user manually disconnects (or reboots). It should time out, roll back the WFP/DNS changes, and/or clearly offer "disable Kill Switch" instead of leaving the machine offline.
2. **Route monitor defects** in the same successful log:
   - `Adding exclusion route for /999999` → `Failed to update route: 87` (ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER) — an invalid prefix is produced while parsing the configuration.

3. **LAN breakage**: the same log captures `192.168.0.0/24`, `172.25.64.0/20`, `172.30.208.0/20` and the resulting table routes them via the tunnel, so the local router/Docker/WSL become unreachable while connected (cf. #2830). Separate from Kill Switch, but visible in the same session.
