issues.title: Gecko/Salamander PacketConn wrappers disable UDP batching and GSO on Linux
issues.body:
### Summary

The Gecko/Salamander UDP wrappers do not implement the full `OOBCapablePacketConn` interface expected by the bundled quic-go. As a result, `wrapConn` selects `basicConn`, losing UDP batch receive and GSO transmit support even when the underlying Linux UDP socket supports them.

This appears to be an optimization integration gap in the obfuscation wrapper. No change to the protocol or the obfuscation wire format seems necessary.

### Environment and method

- Hysteria source tag: `app/v2.14.0`.
- Go: `go1.26.8`, `CGO_ENABLED=0`.
- Linux 6.12.x, ARM64 receiver and amd64 sender.
- Approximately 1 Gbit/s path, approximately 150 ms RTT.
- Gecko with the default 512/1200 handshake size bounds.
- Single QUIC connection. Download tests with 64 MiB stream / 128 MiB connection receive windows to avoid a small flow-control window masking the IO behavior.
- Temporary instrumented builds; CPU profiles cover 20-second intervals. The built-in time-based download test runs for 26 seconds.

### Source-level cause

In `extras/obfs/conn.go`, `obfsPacketConnUDP` forwards `SyscallConn` and socket buffer methods, but does not provide `ReadMsgUDP` / `WriteMsgUDP`. The outer Gecko wrapper in `extras/obfs/gecko.go` also exposes only packet-at-a-time IO.

In the bundled quic-go's `sys_conn.go`, failure of the `OOBCapablePacketConn` assertion selects `basicConn`. Its capabilities do not include GSO. Forwarding `SyscallConn` alone therefore does not preserve the full UDP optimization path.

### Measurements

With the original transport path:

- Built-in download test: approximately 550 Mbit/s.
- Sender CPU profile: approximately 34 CPU-seconds during 20 seconds of wall time.
- The `sendto` call path accounts for approximately 43% of sender CPU samples.
- AES-GCM encryption accounts for approximately 2% of sender CPU samples.

An experimental Linux adapter implements `ReadBatch`, `ReadMsgUDP`, and `WriteMsgUDP`. On GSO sends it obfuscates each segment separately, retains an independent Salamander salt for each resulting datagram, and adjusts `UDP_SEGMENT` for the salt overhead. Long-header packets retain the existing Gecko fragmentation/reassembly behavior.

That experimental build reached approximately 690 Mbit/s in the same built-in workload, with approximately 17 sender CPU-seconds per 20 seconds of wall time. Counters confirmed actual GSO use, averaging roughly 10 datagrams per send.

A separate application-stream control, keeping an unmodified sing-box 1.14.4 client and its configuration fixed, gave approximately 550–560 Mbit/s with the original server path and 710–730 Mbit/s with the experimental server in repeated runs.

**Attribution limit:** the experimental build also replaces the scalar Salamander XOR loop with equivalent word-wise operations. These measurements compare the combined build; they are not an isolated GSO-only benchmark. A receiver-only XOR control produced only a small throughput change, approximately 550 to 570 Mbit/s. Lock-contention profiles did not identify the obfuscator locks as the dominant wait.

### Reproduction outline

1. Run two standard endpoints with Gecko, the receive windows above, and the normal BBR download path.
2. Run `hysteria speedtest --duration 26s --skip-upload` using the normal client configuration.
3. Inspect which raw-connection implementation quic-go selected and capture a sender CPU profile.
4. Compare with a segment-aware batch/GSO adapter, checking both payload throughput and actual batch/GSO counters.

The existing obfuscation tests plus additional Linux tests verified unchanged salted XOR bytes, independent GSO datagram boundaries, and bidirectional interoperability with the original Gecko wrapper, including handshake reassembly.

### Requested direction

Would an opt-in Linux batch/GSO-capable obfuscation adapter be acceptable? It would need explicit segment-aware obfuscation rather than simply exposing the raw socket, and production review for PMTU, ECN/ancillary metadata, fallback

issues.title: fix(acl): allow hyphens in outbound names
issues.body:
ACL rules are parsed with `linePattern` in `extras/outbounds/acl/parse.go`, which only accepts `\w+` as the outbound name, so a rule like `New-turkey(geosite:cn)` fails with "invalid syntax" even though the server config happily accepts an outbound with that name. After parsing, the name is only used for a lowercased map lookup, so allowing `-` in the pattern is all it takes.

I kept this to hyphens as the issue describes. Names with other characters such as dots still don't parse, same as before.

The new `TestParseTextRules` case fails on master with `invalid syntax at line 2: New-turkey(geosite:cn)` and passes with this change. `gofumpt -l -extra .` is clean, and `go test ./...` passes in `extras/outbounds` and `app/cmd`.

Fixes #1323
